Formulate and solve an optimal power flow problem on the MATPOWER distribution microgrid test case \(\texttt{case33mg}\). The network data must first be modified as follows: (i) set the shunt susceptance \(B_S\) at Bus 20 to 0.2 (in the case data units), (ii) set the minimum voltage magnitude \(V_{\min}\) at Bus 17 to 1.0 p.u., (iii) scale the series reactance \(X\) of Branch (from Bus 1 to Bus 14) by a factor of 1.2, and (iv) scale the series resistance \(R\) of Branch (from Bus 2 to Bus 18) by a factor of 1.1. 

The core optimization is an AC OPF economic dispatch that minimizes the standard MATPOWER generation cost subject to full AC power flow equations, generator operating limits, voltage magnitude limits, and branch flow limits. In addition, introduce an explicit reactive power reserve variable for each generator, representing the unused reactive capability. Enforce generator-level reactive reserve capacity coupling by requiring \(Q_g + Q_{res} \le Q_{max}\) for each generator, and impose a system-wide reactive reserve requirement such that the total reactive reserve is at least 10% of total active load \(\sum P_d\). Add an additional (linear) incentive term to the objective to encourage maintaining reactive reserves by assigning a negative linear cost to \(Q_{res}\).

Also impose a CO2 emission cap constraint on active generation dispatch using generator-specific linear emission factors \(e_i\) (tCO2/MWh), enforcing \(\sum_i e_i P_{g,i} \le \text{Cap}\) (in t/h for a 1-hour period). If the case has more generators than the example factors provided, apply the available factors cyclically across generators.

Implement the model using MATPOWER's OPF model construction interface (OPF setup with an optimization model), adding the new variables, linear constraints, and the additional cost term. Finally, solve with an AC OPF solver (MIPS) and set the OPF feasibility tolerance \(\texttt{opf.violation}=1\text{e-}8\).

Solve an Optimal Transmission Switching (OTS) optimal power flow for the MATPOWER test system case22. The decision problem uses a DC power flow network model with transmission switching modeled via binary line-status variables. The objective is to minimize the standard generation cost augmented by an additional quadratic reactive power procurement cost proxy associated with line charging susceptance, represented as a bus-voltage-squared penalty aggregated from incident branch charging terms.

Apply the following parameter modifications to the case data prior to optimization: (1) set the reactive demand at bus 8 (QD) to zero; (2) set the minimum reactive power limit (QMIN) of the generator connected to bus 1 to −50 MVAr; (3) double the series resistance BR_R of branch from bus 11 to bus 19; and (4) scale the total line charging susceptance BR_B of the branch from bus 22 to bus 1 by 1.1.

The OTS formulation introduces, for each branch, a continuous active power flow variable and a binary switching variable indicating whether the line is in service. It replaces the standard DC branch flow equations with big-M constraints that enforce consistency between bus voltage angles and branch flows when a line is on, while relaxing them when the line is switched off. Thermal line limits are enforced conditionally on the switching status so that a switched-off line carries zero flow. Power balance is enforced using the added line flow variables and generator injections. A global limit is imposed on the number of lines that may be switched off.

In addition, augment the objective with a quadratic term that penalizes voltage magnitude squared at each bus with coefficients derived from incident branch charging susceptances (a proxy cost for reactive power associated with line charging). This term is added to the standard OPF objective.

Implement the model using MATPOWER’s OPF model builder, adding the required variables, linear constraints, and quadratic cost. Use solver settings such that the OPF feasibility/constraint violation tolerance is 1e−6, and solve the resulting mixed-integer program with the DC OPF solver configured for OTS (via an MILP/MIP backend), while keeping the specified time/node limits and heuristic settings for the integer solver.

Using a PTDF-based linear flow model, enforce that for every in-service branch, the worst-case post-uncertainty absolute flow remains within the branch RATE_A limit. The planning horizon is defined by the time-series profiles that scale load and renewable availability, resulting in a multi-interval optimization with inter-temporal generator commitment logic. The objective is to minimize total operating cost over the horizon, including energy production costs, commitment-related start-up and shut-down costs, and additional penalty terms introduced for softening line flow limits.

In addition to the original generation cost objective provided in the case, augment the objective by adding a “system average branch loadability” penalty term. This added term is the average across all branches of the ratio between each branch’s apparent power magnitude and its long-term thermal rating RATE_A. The apparent power for each branch is computed as the average of the sending-end and receiving-end apparent power magnitudes. For branches with RATE_A equal to 0 (unset), treat their rating as 250 MVA for the purpose of this penalty. The penalty weight is lambda_load = 1.

Implement the augmented objective using a nonlinear cost component that depends on the OPF decision variables through AC network power flow quantities. Formulate and solve a DC Optimal Power Flow with Optimal Transmission Switching (DC-OTS) on the MATPOWER test case “case22”. The model uses DC power flow physics with bus voltage angles as state variables and active power balance at each bus. In addition to the standard generation dispatch decision, the problem endogenously determines the on/off status of each transmission line via binary switching variables, using a big-M linearization to couple line flows, angle differences, and the switch status.

Apply the following data (parameter) modifications to the base case before building the optimization model: (1) set the reactive load at bus 8 (QD) to zero; (2) set the generator reactive minimum limit (QMIN) for the generator at bus 1 to −50 MVAr; (3) scale the resistance BR_R of the branch from bus 11 to bus 19 by a factor of 2; and (4) scale the total line charging susceptance BR_B of the branch from bus 22 to bus 1 by a factor of 1.1. Although the optimization model is DC, these edits are still applied to the case data exactly as specified.

Augment the DC-OTS model with reserve scheduling decisions and costs. Introduce continuous reserve variables for each generator: up regulation reserve, down regulation reserve, spinning reserve, and non-spinning reserve. Enforce generator headroom and footroom constraints so that scheduled energy plus upward reserves do not exceed PMAX, and energy minus down reserves stays above PMIN. Impose system-wide reserve requirements for each reserve type equal to 1% of the total system real power demand (in MW). Add a linear reserve procurement cost term to the objective with specified per-MW prices for each reserve type, combined with the existing generation cost objective from the OPF.

Additionally, include a regional spinning-style requirement based on two regions of generators. Define regions as generator index sets {1,2} and {3}. For each region, require that the sum of up-regulation reserve plus spinning reserve scheduled by generators in that region meets or exceeds an exogenous requirement. Use regional requirements of (RU, SP) in MW equal to [50, 20] for region 1 and [100, 100] for region 2. Enforce per-generator maximum eligibility limits for RU and SP (e.g., 100 MW each) and allow all generators to participate.

Solve the resulting mixed-integer linear program (MILP) DC-OTS with reserves using MATPOWER’s OPF modeling layer, using an integer-capable solver (via “OT” with intlinprog settings). Use a strict feasibility/constraint tolerance by setting opf_violation to 1e-6, and limit the MILP runtime and search via maximum time and maximum nodes settings; report solution status, objective value, line switching decisions, dispatch, and reserve schedules.

Formulate and solve a DC Optimal Transmission Switching (DC-OTS) optimal power flow on the MATPOWER IEEE 118-bus test system (case118). The decision-making problem co-optimizes generator real-power dispatch and binary line switching statuses to minimize total generation operating cost while meeting DC power balance and network security limits.

Modeling begins from the standard case118 data, with a parameter modification applied to represent a changed shunt element: at bus 78, the shunt susceptance BS is set to −0.1 (in the case data’s per-unit shunt susceptance convention). All other case data remain unchanged.

The DC-OTS structure introduces, for every branch, (i) an explicit real-power flow variable and (ii) a binary on/off switching variable. DC nodal power balance is enforced using an incidence-based relationship between branch flows and generator injections. Line thermal limits are enforced with switching-dependent bounds such that, when a line is opened, its flow is forced to zero; when it is closed, the flow must lie within its DC limit. The switching-physics coupling between bus phase angles and branch flows is enforced using big-M constraints so that the DC flow-angle relationship is active only when the line is on.

In addition to the original generation cost, the objective is augmented with a voltage-stability-related nonlinear penalty based on the L-index. The L-index is computed from the network admittance matrix via F = −Y_LL^{-1} Y_LG, where generator buses (REF/PV) form set G and load buses (PQ) form set L, and the cost uses L_max = max_j L_j over PQ buses. This adds a scalar nonlinear cost term lambda_L * L_max(V) to the optimization objective.

Frequency-security constraints are also added using reserve-like decision variables. A scalar proxy variable represents the largest online generator output (max-trip proxy) and per-generator reserve variables represent headroom. Constraints enforce (a) each generator output is not greater than the max-trip proxy, (b) each generator output plus its reserve does not exceed its nameplate maximum, (c) a RoCoF-based upper bound on the max-trip proxy derived from an aggregate inertia model, and (d) a steady-state frequency drop condition requiring sufficient total reserve relative to the max-trip proxy.

Implementation uses MATPOWER’s OPF modeling layer (opf_setup) with added variables and linear constraints, and a mixed-integer DC solver interface for OTS (intlinprog via MP-Opt-Model). The nonlinear L-index term is attached as an additional nonlinear cost function component. Use a strict OPF feasibility tolerance by setting opf.violation = 1e-6, and set appropriate MILP time/node limits for intlinprog. Because the objective includes a nonlinear term, the implementation solves the MIP with the OTS formulation and evaluates/penalizes the L-index through the nonlinear cost callback as provided, expecting the solver configuration to be compatible with the selected approach; if the chosen MIP solver cannot use nonlinear callbacks, solve the OTS MIP first and then post-process (or iterate with outer approximation). Solver verbosity should be enabled for diagnostics, and maximum runtime/node limits should be applied as specified in the options.
